questions.q: What does ethers v6's BrowserProvider wrap?
options: Whatever EIP-1193 provider the browser injects, such as window.ethereum from MetaMask
A dedicated backend API server the frontend must run
The subgraph's GraphQL endpoint
A hardcoded list of RPC URLs with no wallet involved
questions.explain: BrowserProvider is built specifically to wrap an injected EIP-1193 provider like window.ethereum, letting the frontend read chain state and, via getSigner(), request signatures from the connected wallet.

questions.q: Why must the frontend send the approve transaction and wait for it to confirm before sending listItem?
options: There's no real reason -- it would work in either order
listItem's own require checks confirm the marketplace already has an approval; sending it before approve confirms would fail that check
approve and listItem must always be combined into a single transaction
listItem doesn't require any approval at all
questions.explain: Lesson 9's listItem requires that the marketplace is already approved (via isApprovedForAll or getApproved) before it will record a listing, so the approval transaction has to land first.

questions.q: In the buy flow, where should the value passed to buyItem come from?
options: The user manually typing in a price
A random number generator
The price field returned by the indexer for that specific listing, passed through unchanged
Half of the listing's price, since the contract adds the rest automatically
questions.explain: The contract's require(msg.value == listing.price, ...) rejects anything that doesn't match exactly, so the frontend should pass the indexer's own price value rather than letting a user retype it.

questions.q: Why does the marketplace page fetch listings from the indexer instead of calling the contract directly in a loop?
options: Calling a contract from a frontend is technically impossible
The indexer replaces the need for the contract entirely
There's no difference in behavior either way
It's faster and already structured for 'all active listings,' which the contract itself has no function for -- the contract remains the source of truth that buyItem still checks on-chain
questions.explain: The indexer gives a fast, pre-aggregated view ('active listings sorted by price'); the contract is still authoritative, which is why buyItem independently re-validates the listing on-chain regardless of what the index shows.

questions.q: What does parseEther do in the listing flow?
options: Fetches the current ETH/USD exchange rate
Converts a human-readable price string like "0.5" into the wei-denominated uint256 the contract's listItem expects
Signs the transaction on behalf of the user
Converts wei back into a human-readable string
questions.explain: parseEther converts a decimal ETH amount into the integer wei value Solidity's uint256 price parameter expects; formatEther does the reverse conversion when displaying a price.
